items.question: A sports media company runs live match commentary summarisation. At the Saturday afternoon peak, consumption sits at 88% of the account's provisioned throughput allocation. The product director has just committed publicly to shipping a fan-sentiment panel for the start of next season, which will call the model once per minute per live match on the same allocation. Engineering has not yet estimated its demand. As architect, what should you do next?

options.A: Provision additional worker pods and raise the autoscaler ceiling now, so the new panel has somewhere to run the moment the season opens.
options.B: Move the existing summarisation traffic to a cheaper tier to create allocation room for the new sentiment panel before the season opens.
options.C: Estimate the new feature's token demand at peak concurrent match count, compare it against the remaining 12% of headroom, and take that to the allocation decision.
options.D: Defer the capacity question until consumption actually reaches the allocation ceiling, since meaningful headroom still exists at today's peak.

items.question: A property-management SaaS provider serves 1,200 landlord tenants from one deployment. A response cache in front of its lease-question assistant is keyed on a hash of the normalised question text plus the model version. A support engineer has confirmed a case where one tenant received an answer quoting another tenant's bespoke lease addendum, because both had asked a similarly worded question and the retrieval scope differs per tenant. What is the correct fix?

options.A: Shorten the cache entry lifetime to a few minutes so cross-tenant entries expire quickly and the exposure window stays small.
options.B: Extend the cache key to include every input that changes the output — tenant identifier and retrieval scope — and accept the lower hit rate.
options.C: Encrypt cache entries at rest with a per-tenant key from the key vault, so entries cannot be read across tenant boundaries.
options.D: Add a post-retrieval filter that strips any content in a cached response that does not belong to the requesting tenant before it is returned.

items.question: An academic publisher processes 14 content types — journal articles, conference abstracts, book chapters and others — each with its own model tier, prompt variant, retrieval scope and output schema. All of it lives in a 2,000-line dispatch function of nested conditionals that has grown over two years. Adding a fifteenth content type is estimated at four days, and two of the last three additions caused production incidents by changing behaviour for an existing type. The team has capacity for one substantial refactor this quarter. What should it be?

options.A: Split the dispatch function into 14 handler classes, one per content type, each owning its tier, prompt and schema behind a common interface.
options.B: Add characterisation unit tests around the existing dispatch function so behaviour changes to existing types are caught before release.
options.C: Replace the conditionals with a declarative per-type configuration validated at load, plus a table-driven evaluation that runs every type on every change.
options.D: Have a small model classify the incoming document at ingest and select tier, prompt and schema dynamically, removing the need to maintain a mapping at all.

items.question: A waste-management group is automating the coding of supplier invoices to internal cost categories. The sponsor has set a 99% accuracy acceptance criterion. Baseline measurement shows the incumbent clerical process codes 93% of invoices to the category a senior reviewer would choose, and that two senior reviewers independently disagree with each other on 4% of invoices. The team's system currently measures 91%. What should the architect propose?

options.A: Accept the 99% criterion as written and route every invoice through human review before posting, so the number is met from day one.
options.B: Re-anchor the criterion on the measured baseline: define ground truth by adjudicated labels and target parity with the 93% incumbent at materially lower unit cost.
options.C: Tighten the coding rubric until senior reviewers agree with each other consistently, then re-measure the incumbent process and set the target from the improved figure.
options.D: Decline the use case, since 91% measured against a 99% requirement is too large a gap to close within the current model's capability.

items.question: A mining services firm runs two workloads through one worker pool with a shared concurrency limit: interactive geology queries averaging 1.1 seconds, and full drill-report analyses that take three to six minutes each. Interactive queries show a p95 of 14 seconds even though the queries themselves are consistently fast. The upstream throughput allocation is already the binding constraint at peak, so the shared concurrency limit cannot be raised. What is the correct design change?

options.A: Chunk the drill reports into smaller sections so each unit of work occupies a concurrency slot for seconds rather than minutes.
options.B: Move the drill-report analyses to a faster tier so they finish sooner and release their concurrency slots earlier.
options.C: Partition the concurrency limit into a reserved interactive share and a bounded long-job share, so short queries never queue behind a long analysis.
options.D: Raise the interactive queries' priority in the existing queue so they are dequeued ahead of the analyses whenever a slot frees.

items.question: A pipeline runs four model calls in strict sequence. Which structural change most reliably improves its end-to-end tail latency?

options.A: Removing a stage, or running two stages that do not depend on each other concurrently.
options.B: Raising the concurrency limit of the worker pool that executes the four pipeline calls.
options.C: Enabling response streaming on each of the four calls so tokens arrive at the caller earlier.
options.D: Adding a retry with exponential backoff at each stage so slow responses are replaced by fast ones.

items.question: An architect is challenged on why the capacity plan for a Claude-based service is not expressed simply in requests per second. What is the strongest justification?

options.A: Requests per second is a client-side metric and cannot be measured reliably at the service boundary, so the plan would rest on unverifiable numbers.
options.B: Two workloads at the same request rate can consume order-of-magnitude different capacity, because tokens and slot occupancy govern consumption.
options.C: Requests per second ignores failed and retried requests, so the plan would systematically under-count the real offered load.
options.D: Request rates vary by region, so a single figure cannot represent a multi-region deployment with different peak hours.

items.question: A metropolitan transport authority has run a journey-disruption assistant for 14 months. Adding a new disruption category — a change that touches wording and one output field — now takes three weeks and two rounds of manual spot-checking, and the team cannot say in advance which existing behaviours a wording change will disturb. Which TWO practices would most reduce the cost of behavioural change in this system? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: An executable evaluation suite run on every prompt change, so the effect of a wording edit on existing behaviours is measured rather than argued about.
options.B: Writing longer and more exhaustive prompts up front, so that future disruption categories are already covered by the existing instructions.
options.C: A single canonical output-schema definition that generates both the prompt's format instruction and the consumer's parser, so a field change is one edit.
options.D: Moving every stage to the highest-capability tier, since stronger instruction-following reduces how often the prompts need editing at all.
options.E: Storing prompts as free text in a database so operations staff can adjust wording between releases without waiting for a deploy.

items.question: An appliance manufacturer is designing a warranty-fraud pre-screen. It receives about 9,000 warranty claims a week. The fraud team can investigate at most 400 referrals a week and will not be expanded. The compliance sponsor requires that the pre-screen surface at least 95% of fraudulent claims. Which TWO conclusions follow from these constraints? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Referral capacity fixes the number of positives the system may emit, so the model must be tuned as precision at a fixed referral volume rather than optimised for overall accuracy.
options.B: The two requirements are only jointly satisfiable if measured fraud prevalence is below roughly 4.7%, since capturing 95% of fraud within 400 referrals implies 0.95 x 9,000 x prevalence cannot exceed 400.
options.C: Overall accuracy is the correct headline metric here, because it weighs missed fraud and false referrals in a single number the sponsor can track each week.
options.D: Because recall is the binding compliance requirement, the design should maximise recall and let the weekly referral volume find its own level.
options.E: Moving the pre-screen to a higher-capability tier satisfies both constraints regardless of prevalence, because a stronger model separates fraud cleanly enough to fit the capacity.

items.question: In a pipeline that deliberately mixes model tiers to control cost, which stage most justifies the highest-capability tier?

options.A: The stage handling the largest share of request volume, since improving the common case matters most in aggregate.
options.B: The first stage, so that every later stage receives the cleanest possible input to work with.
options.C: The stage whose errors cannot be detected or corrected by any later stage in the pipeline.
options.D: The stage with the longest prompt, since context length is what most strains a smaller tier's attention.

items.question: What most strongly justifies imposing a hard cap on input tokens per request in a high-volume production system?

options.A: It materially reduces the average cost per request, since most requests already sit close to the cap and would be trimmed by it.
options.B: A small fraction of requests carries a disproportionate share of tokens, so a cap bounds worst-case cost and slot occupancy.
options.C: It improves answer quality, because shorter prompts are consistently easier for the model to follow instruction by instruction.
options.D: It is a prerequisite for enabling response streaming reliably, since the server sizes its output buffer from the input length.

items.question: An Australian energy retailer runs a bill-explanation service. Its application tier and retrieval index are hosted in Sydney, but all model traffic routes through the company's own API gateway deployed in Virginia, a legacy of the original build. The flow makes three sequential model calls, and each pays roughly 180 ms of cross-Pacific round trip. Measured end-to-end p95 is 2,700 ms against an internal budget of 2,500 ms. The three calls are genuinely dependent — each consumes the previous one's output. What is the most effective change?

options.A: Move the gateway to the Sydney region alongside the callers, removing roughly 540 ms of pure transit from the critical path.
options.B: Add a regional read cache in Sydney for the responses of the first of the three calls, so repeat bills skip it.
options.C: Keep the gateway where it is and shorten the generated output of each of the three calls to recover the 200 ms overrun.
options.D: Replicate the retrieval index into Virginia so retrieval and model traffic are co-located in one region.

items.question: An online auction platform generates a listing description when a seller submits an item. p50 is 900 ms and p99 is 5,400 ms, and the p99 is what sellers complain about — the generation itself is read-only and has no side effects. The team must bring the p99 inside 2,500 ms without changing the model tier or the output length, and has been told any solution must add no more than about 5% to token spend. Which approach fits?

options.A: Set a 2,500 ms client timeout and retry once on expiry, so no seller ends up waiting longer than the stated budget.
options.B: Issue a duplicate request once the original has been outstanding for about the p95 elapsed time, take the first to finish and cancel the other.
options.C: Issue two requests concurrently for every submission and take the first to complete, which halves the chance of any submission hitting a slow response.
options.D: Raise the client concurrency limit so a slow generation no longer delays the submissions queued behind it.

items.question: A national tax authority runs a filing-help assistant. Analysis of last season shows that during the ten-week filing peak, about 60% of questions map to a known set of roughly 2,000 standard topics; the remaining 40% is long tail. The standard topics change only when the authority publishes revised guidance, which happens a few times a year on a scheduled date. Peak throughput demand is the authority's binding constraint. Which TWO statements about precomputing answers for the standard set are correct? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Precomputing the standard set off-peak converts variable peak inference into fixed off-peak work and removes roughly 60% of question volume from the peak throughput demand.
options.B: Precomputed answers must be regenerated and re-evaluated whenever revised guidance is published, so the job belongs in the publication pipeline rather than in a cron.
options.C: Given filing-season volumes, precomputation raises total token spend, because every one of the 2,000 standard topics is generated whether or not it is asked.
options.D: Precomputation removes the need for a live model path during the filing peak, since the standard set covers the overwhelming majority of real demand.
options.E: Because the answers are generated in advance and reviewed once before publication, they no longer need to carry citations back to the guidance they came from.

items.question: A hospital group's platform team is building shared infrastructure for six clinical and administrative teams that will call Claude. The CTO wants to avoid being locked in and has asked for an abstraction layer that would let any model vendor be substituted. The platform lead points out that a genuinely vendor-neutral interface would have to reduce to a lowest common denominator, giving up tool-use semantics and prompt-structure features the teams already depend on, and that the translation layer would itself become a shared dependency for six teams. What should the architect recommend?

options.A: Build the vendor-neutral interface as requested and have all six teams work within the common subset, since portability is worth more than any individual feature.
options.B: Place the seam at the task boundary: expose internal capability services with stable contracts, and keep provider-specific features behind them.
options.C: Call the provider SDK directly from each of the six team codebases, accepting that meaningful portability is not achievable in practice.
options.D: Maintain parallel implementations against two providers so the switch is exercised continuously and lock-in never accumulates.

items.question: An airline's disruption-rebooking assistant costs a measured $0.011 per request, on a call carrying about 6,000 input tokens of policy and itinerary context and returning about 500 output tokens. Product wants to add a short passenger-facing explanation of why the offered alternative was chosen. It reuses the same context and adds roughly 300 output tokens to the existing call; a prototype measures the increment at $0.0026. Finance has priced the feature in the business case at $0.011 per use, using the current average cost per request. How should the architect respond?

options.A: Accept the $0.011 figure as a conservative estimate, since costing at the current average avoids understating the feature's contribution to spend.
options.B: Price the feature at the marginal $0.0026, since the average embeds retrieval and 6,000 shared input tokens it never re-incurs; flag the 300 output tokens as latency.
options.C: Treat the feature as effectively free, since it reuses an existing call, adds no new request to the system and consumes no additional retrieval.
options.D: Keep the average-cost figure for consistency with how every other feature in the business case is priced, and note the discrepancy in a footnote for the investment committee.

items.question: In a system that must remain within a provisioned throughput allocation, why is it better to make the admission-control decision at the edge rather than in the worker that issues the model call?

options.A: The edge has better observability, so shed decisions can be logged with the full request context and surfaced in one dashboard.
options.B: Workers cannot return an error response to the client once they have begun processing a request and issued the model call.
options.C: By the time a request reaches a worker it has already claimed a concurrency slot and spent retrieval budget.
options.D: Edge infrastructure is cheaper to operate per request than worker infrastructure, so shedding there costs less.

items.question: A food manufacturer screens about 120,000 consumer complaints a month for potential allergen incidents. A cheap first-stage filter measures 0.99 recall and 0.12 precision. Measured prevalence of genuine allergen incidents in the complaint stream is 1.5%. Complaints passed by the filter go to a second, far more expensive verification stage. Which THREE statements follow from these figures? (Choose THREE.)

options.A: The second stage will see roughly 14,850 complaints a month — about 12% of total volume — and that is the figure its cost and capacity model must be built on.
options.B: End-to-end recall cannot exceed the first stage's 0.99, so any requirement above 99% detection is infeasible without changing the first stage.
options.C: The first stage's 0.12 precision is not a defect: its job is to shed the clearly-negative majority of volume cheaply, and precision is the second stage's responsibility.
options.D: Raising the first stage's precision from 0.12 to 0.50 would improve end-to-end recall, because fewer false positives leaves the second stage more capacity per case.
options.E: Because the first stage has 0.99 recall, the system as a whole will detect 99% of incidents regardless of how the second verification stage behaves.

items.question: What must be true for a cheap-tier-first cascade with escalation to a higher tier to be a sound design rather than a way of making mistakes cheaply?

options.A: The cheap tier must emit a reliable signal — a calibrated confidence, a verification check or a structural test — showing when to escalate.
options.B: Both tiers must run the same prompt, so their outputs stay directly comparable at the escalation boundary.
options.C: The escalation rate must stay below 50%, or the blended cost rises above flat routing and the advantage disappears.
options.D: The cheap tier must have the same context window as the higher tier, so no case is ever rejected before it is scored.

items.question: A car-sharing operator uses one model-driven assessment of vehicle-return photographs to drive two automated actions: raising a maintenance job for a depot technician, who reviews the photos before acting, and charging a damage fee to the member's payment card, which the member can dispute and which is reportable to the consumer regulator if disputes exceed a threshold. The product director has asked for "one accuracy target for the AI" to simplify reporting. Which TWO responses are correct? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Accuracy requirements should be set per action according to how reversible it is and what an error costs, so the fee-charging path needs a materially higher bar and a review threshold.
options.B: One underlying assessment can drive both actions provided the confidence threshold and the escalation rule are configured separately per action.
options.C: A single system-wide target set to the stricter of the two is the safer default, because it cannot under-protect either path or either action.
options.D: Since the fee path carries the higher risk, moving it to the highest model tier is the primary control for meeting its accuracy requirement.
options.E: Reversibility is a legal characteristic rather than an architectural input, so it belongs in the terms of service and the dispute process rather than in the system design.

items.question: A classified-ads marketplace earns an average of $0.040 per listing and has set a moderation budget of 2.25% of that, giving a hard ceiling of $0.0009 per listing for automated listing-quality checks. The current design sends every listing to a model and measures $0.0031 per listing. Analysis of a week of listings shows that about 75% are from established sellers reusing prior categories and templates, and are resolved correctly by deterministic rules the team already has. What design meets the ceiling?

options.A: Sample 25% of listings for model-based moderation and pass the remainder unchecked, which also brings the blended cost to about $0.00078 per listing.
options.B: Route through the deterministic rules first and send only the roughly 25% they cannot resolve to the model, at a blended $0.00078 per listing.
options.C: Move the existing design to the cheapest available tier and accept the resulting quality reduction across all listings, including the difficult ones.
options.D: Open a commercial negotiation for a lower per-call rate, since a 3.4-fold gap is unlikely to be closed by design changes alone at this volume.

items.question: A fashion e-commerce brand has committed publicly to launching an AI personal stylist to its 2 million registered customers in twelve weeks. The team is debating whether it should be a single call with a large catalogue context, a multi-step agent with catalogue tools, or a two-tier cascade — and has already begun a spike on all three. Nothing about actual demand has been measured: there is no figure for sessions per user, turns per session, or tokens per turn. The architect has one week before the design must be fixed. What should happen first?

options.A: Pick the multi-step agent with catalogue tools, since it is the most capable option and can be simplified later if it proves too expensive.
options.B: Open the throughput allocation increase with the vendor now, because lead times are long and capacity is the one thing that cannot be added late in a launch.
options.C: Ship a deliberately simple version to a small invited cohort and measure sessions per user, turns per session and tokens per turn before fixing the design.
options.D: Design the caching layer first, since it is common to all three candidate architectures and will reduce peak demand whichever one is chosen.

items.question: An architect wants a single tracked metric that reflects whether a Claude-based system is becoming harder or easier to change over time. Which is the most useful?

options.A: Total prompt line count across every prompt in the system, tracked month over month against a rolling baseline.
options.B: The number of distinct prompt files checked into the platform repository, counted at each release.
options.C: Elapsed time from starting a typical behavioural change to it being safely in production, plus how many components it touched.
options.D: The number of distinct model tiers and provider endpoints the system depends on in production.

items.question: A semiconductor fab classifies yield-excursion reports into root-cause families. A single call measures 88% agreement with the engineering panel's adjudicated label. Sampling the same call three times and taking the majority measures 92%, at 3.1 times the token cost including the short aggregation step. The three samples can be issued concurrently. The fab must decide whether to adopt this before the next process node ramps. Which TWO conclusions are sound? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: The gain is bounded by how independent the errors are: where the model is confidently wrong all three samples agree, so the four-point improvement is the ceiling of this technique.
options.B: Because the samples run concurrently, the added latency is roughly the aggregation step rather than three sequential generations, so this trades cost for accuracy far more than latency.
options.C: Majority voting makes the classification deterministic across runs, which resolves the reproducibility concerns that come with sampling the model repeatedly.
options.D: Moving from three samples to five should deliver roughly double the improvement, since the gain scales with the number of independent opinions collected.
options.E: Voting improves worst-case behaviour by guaranteeing that every classification has been independently checked twice before the label is emitted.

items.question: An international development NGO has an eight-person engineering team and ten weeks to deliver grant-application triage before the next funding round opens. A vendor product covers the requirement on month-to-month terms with a documented data export. The programme director argues that triage logic could eventually become the NGO's distinctive capability and that building it now avoids paying twice. The team has never run this workload and has no data on application volume, mix or failure modes. What should the architect recommend?

options.A: Build now, because a capability that may become the NGO's distinctive advantage should not be outsourced at the point it is being defined.
options.B: Buy on the month-to-month terms, put a thin internal contract in front of it, and set an explicit trigger at which building is re-evaluated.
options.C: Buy, but negotiate a three-year term to secure the discount, since the capability is clearly needed for the long run and the rate improves with term.
options.D: Build a provider-neutral internal platform now and run the vendor behind it, so any later switch is invisible to the consuming teams.

items.question: A team reports that a proposed reranking stage "costs 40 ms". Before accepting that figure into an end-to-end latency budget, what most needs to be established?

options.A: Whether 40 ms is a mean or a tail figure, and whether it was measured under production load.
options.B: Whether the reranker runs in the same language runtime and process as the rest of the retrieval service.
options.C: Whether the measurement was taken after the process and its local caches had fully warmed up.
options.D: Whether the reranker process is co-located on the same host as the retrieval index it queries.

items.question: A ticketing platform caches assistant answers keyed on normalised question text. When a stadium tour goes on sale, roughly 40,000 users ask essentially the same question about queue position within ninety seconds. Because the key is cold at the moment the on-sale opens, the first wave of requests all miss simultaneously and issue their own generation, saturating the throughput allocation and pushing p95 past two minutes. The cache then fills and the incident resolves. The on-sale for the next tour is in six days. What should the team do next?

options.A: Increase the cache entry lifetime so the queue-position key stays warm for far longer between on-sale events.
options.B: Add request coalescing on the cache key so only one generation runs per key and concurrent misses wait on that result.
options.C: Pre-warm the cache with every question the platform has ever seen, in a batch job that runs just before each on-sale opens.
options.D: Add worker capacity for the on-sale window so the wave of concurrent misses can all be absorbed at once.

items.question: A public broadcaster has been offered a twelve-month committed-throughput contract by its provider, discounted against on-demand rates in exchange for a monthly minimum. Its measured demand has a peak-to-average ratio of about five to one, driven by breaking-news surges. Two further facts are on the table: the engineering roadmap includes a context-restructuring change in the second quarter that the team believes will cut tokens per request substantially, and the newsroom is piloting two features whose adoption is genuinely uncertain. How should the commitment be sized?

options.A: Size it to the forecast peak, since the discount applies across the whole commitment and peak coverage maximises the total saving.
options.B: Take no commitment this year, because the second-quarter roadmap change and the pilot uncertainty make any figure a guess.
options.C: Size it to the average of the twelve-month forecast, which balances the breaking-news surges against the quiet periods between them.
options.D: Size it to the floor of demand the broadcaster is confident it will consume even if both pilots fail and the token cut lands, and buy the rest on demand.

items.question: A utility's field-service platform gives technicians a job-summary assistant on ruggedised tablets over cellular. The service-side p95, measured at the API gateway, is 1.2 s against a 1.5 s SLO, and the dashboard has been green for months. Technicians report waits of four to six seconds and have started skipping the feature. Client telemetry, newly added, shows a median 1.1 s of cellular round trip and 1.9 s spent parsing and rendering the response on the tablet. What is the correct response?

options.A: Optimise the model call further, since the 1.2 s service time is the largest single component the team controls directly.
options.B: Enable streaming so the tablet can begin painting content before the full response has arrived over the cellular network.
options.C: Treat the client telemetry as unrepresentative until it has been validated, since the service-side measurement has been stable for months.
options.D: Re-write the SLO at the boundary the technician experiences and split the budget across transport, service and render.

items.question: A bicycle manufacturer extracts specifications from supplier datasheets at 40,000 documents a month. Two options have been measured. On the cheaper tier, token cost is $0.00042 per call, 22% of outputs fail schema validation and are retried once, and 6% of the documents that do pass are wrong in ways caught later by a procurement analyst at a measured $1.80 per correction. On the higher tier, token cost is $0.0021 per call, retries are negligible, and 0.8% require analyst correction at the same $1.80. Procurement has asked which is cheaper.

options.A: The cheaper tier, since its token cost is roughly five times lower and analyst correction is a fixed overhead of the process on either path.
options.B: The two are within noise of each other once the retry rate is included, so the decision should be made on latency and throughput instead.
options.C: The higher tier: cost per document is about $0.109 on the cheaper tier against about $0.017 on the higher tier, because analyst correction dominates token cost.
options.D: It depends on volume: the cheaper tier wins at low monthly volumes and the higher tier wins once volume is large enough for the correction cost to dominate the total.

items.question: A worker pool that issues model calls is fed by an unbounded in-memory queue. What does the lack of a bound guarantee once arrival rate exceeds service rate for a sustained period?

options.A: Wait time grows without limit while the system reports no errors, so callers time out and abandon requests workers still execute.
options.B: Throughput degrades gradually and proportionally, giving operators a smooth signal to act on before it gets bad.
options.C: Requests begin to be served out of order, because an in-memory queue reorders under sustained pressure.
options.D: Memory exhaustion is the only real consequence, and it can be managed by sizing the worker host generously.

items.question: A genealogical records service expects traffic to grow roughly fourfold over the next year as it opens two new markets. Today, at current traffic, the provisioned model throughput allocation runs at 60% utilisation at peak and the retrieval index tier runs at 15% CPU at peak. Model calls average 1.8 s and retrieval averages 90 ms. Which capacity action should be planned first, and why?

options.A: Scale the retrieval index tier, because retrieval is invoked on every request and its CPU utilisation will rise in step with traffic growth.
options.B: Nothing yet: both tiers have headroom today, and latency will degrade visibly well before either one reaches saturation.
options.C: Plan both together, since a fourfold increase saturates the two tiers at roughly the same point in the growth curve anyway.
options.D: Plan the model throughput allocation increase: at 60% today it binds at about 1.7 times current traffic, while retrieval at 15% has headroom to about 6.7 times.

items.question: A childcare-centre management SaaS vendor serves 60 enterprise customers. Over three years, 41 of them have acquired at least one free-form prompt override for the incident-report assistant, negotiated during their implementations. A platform-wide behavioural change now requires a specialist to read and manually validate 41 variants, and the last such change took nine weeks. The commercial team will not agree to remove customisation, which is part of how the product is sold. Which TWO changes would most reduce change cost while preserving customisation? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Replace free-form overrides with a bounded set of declared options — tone, jurisdiction, disclaimers, escalation wording — composed into one canonical prompt, so customisation becomes data.
options.B: Run the shared evaluation suite automatically against every active customer configuration on each platform change, so validation scales with compute rather than specialist hours.
options.C: Freeze all existing overrides and migrate every customer onto one canonical prompt at their next contract renewal, ending the variant problem.
options.D: Move each customer's override into a separately deployed instance so a change to one configuration cannot possibly affect another customer.
options.E: Introduce a per-override charge at renewal, so the commercial incentive discourages new variants from being negotiated during implementations.

items.question: A payroll bureau extracts hours, rates and allowance codes from 2.1 million timesheet lines a month submitted as scanned forms and spreadsheets. Extracted values post straight into the payroll engine; no person reads them, and the first sign of an error is a wrong payslip. Adding reviewers at this volume has been ruled out on cost. Errors are individually small but generate statutory correction obligations and union escalations. What should the architecture do?

options.A: Move the extraction to the highest-capability tier, since a lower per-line error rate is the most direct way to cut the number of wrong payslips.
options.B: Add machine-checkable invariants — totals reconciling to gross, rates within contracted bands, hours within rostered limits — so errors surface as exceptions.
options.C: Score every extraction for confidence and route the low-confidence share to a human review queue, accepting that some reviewer capacity must be found after all.
options.D: Log every extraction alongside its source image so that any disputed payslip can be reconstructed and corrected in a later pay run.

items.question: An architect must justify how much capacity headroom to hold above forecast peak demand. What should the headroom be sized from?

options.A: The measured error of the organisation's past demand forecasts, combined with the lead time needed to obtain more capacity.
options.B: A flat 20% margin, which is the conventional allowance for infrastructure capacity planning of this kind.
options.C: The peak-to-average ratio of the workload, since that is the figure describing how variable demand really is.
options.D: The demand of the single largest customer, so that losing or gaining that account does not require a capacity change.

items.question: A stock-photography marketplace has five engineers on its AI team. It needs trace capture across a multi-step pipeline, prompt versioning, a runner for evaluation suites, and per-feature cost reporting. Mature vendor products cover all four. The team lead argues that building in-house avoids a dependency and would take "about two months". What is the soundest recommendation?

options.A: Build all four in-house, because observability of an AI system is too central to outsource and the team would end up extending a vendor's version anyway.
options.B: Build the tracing component in-house, where the multi-step pipeline's structure is bespoke, and buy the other three off the shelf.
options.C: Buy, and treat the vendor's evaluation datasets and rubrics as part of the product, since maintaining them in-house duplicates what the vendor already does well.
options.D: Buy the tooling as undifferentiated infrastructure, but require that evaluation datasets, rubrics and trace history stay owned in-house and exportable.

items.question: A quick-service restaurant chain is designing spoken order-taking for its drive-through lanes. The acoustic requirement is that audible speech must begin within 400 ms of the customer finishing an utterance, or customers talk over the system. The response is rendered by a speech synthesiser that can begin speaking as soon as it has the first few words. Menu, price and availability data are per-store and change daily. Which THREE statements about the latency architecture are correct? (Choose THREE.)

options.A: The binding metric is time to first token, not total generation time, because synthesis can begin on the first tokens and continue while the rest is produced.
options.B: Any retrieval or tool call made after the utterance ends sits inside the 400 ms budget, so menu, price and availability context must be loaded at the start of the conversation.
options.C: A confidence-based cascade that escalates a turn to a higher tier is incompatible with this budget unless the escalation decision is made before generation starts.
options.D: Streaming brings no benefit here, because the consumer of the response is a speech synthesiser rather than a human reader watching the text appear.
options.E: Because each turn produces only a short spoken response, token spend per order is negligible and does not need modelling at estate scale in the business case.

items.question: Why should a cost-per-request dashboard show a high percentile alongside the mean?

options.A: Because the mean cannot be reconciled against a provider invoice line, whereas a high percentile reconciles directly.
options.B: Because percentile cost is far less sensitive to swings in traffic volume than the mean of the same requests.
options.C: Because the distribution is heavy-tailed: the mean hides what a single oversized input or long agent loop can cost.
options.D: Because a high percentile is the standard way to express cost commitments in service level objectives.

items.question: A satellite communications provider runs a Claude-based network-fault triage assistant, currently deployed in one region serving the Americas. It is about to extend to EMEA and APAC operations centres, which run their own shift patterns. APAC engineers on a pilot are seeing roughly 240 ms of additional transit per call. Finance has asked for a single global capacity number to take to the provider this month. What should the architect do next?

options.A: Give finance the sum of the three regions' forecast peaks, which is the safe number and can always be reduced later if it proves generous.
options.B: Deploy in all three regions immediately, since the APAC transit penalty demonstrates that regional presence is required before any capacity number is committed.
options.C: Give finance the current single-region figure multiplied by three, since the three operations centres are similarly sized and staffed.
options.D: Build a per-region demand profile on a common clock, so the three shift-driven peaks can be overlaid and the true global concurrent peak goes to the provider.

items.question: A meal-kit subscription company built a response cache eighteen months ago, when it achieved a 31% hit rate on its recipe-guidance assistant. Since dietary personalisation was added, the hit rate has fallen to 6%. The cache costs roughly a day of engineering attention per release, has been implicated in two incidents where customers saw guidance that ignored a declared allergy after a recipe was updated, and adds a hop to every request. What should the architect recommend?

options.A: Retire the cache: at a 6% hit rate the avoided cost no longer covers the release overhead and correctness risk.
options.B: Re-tune the cache key on normalised question text to raise the hit rate back toward its original level before deciding anything.
options.C: Add semantic matching in front of the exact-match layer to recover the hits lost to wording variation between customers.
options.D: Keep it as it is: a 6% reduction in model calls is still a real saving, and removing live infrastructure carries its own risk.

items.question: A commodities exchange runs an alert-triage assistant on its market-surveillance desk. Each alert must be triaged within 30 seconds of arrival to be useful to the desk. The service sustains 20 alerts per second. During volatile sessions, arrivals exceed that and the queue grows; today the queue is unbounded and the team's proposal is to alert operators when p95 triage latency exceeds 25 seconds. What should the design do instead?

options.A: Keep the unbounded queue but raise the deadline to 60 seconds during declared volatile sessions, so far fewer alerts are counted as late.
options.B: Alert on p95 triage latency as proposed, but at 15 seconds rather than 25, so operators have more time to react before the desk's deadline is breached.
options.C: Add worker capacity dynamically whenever p95 latency rises, so the service rate tracks the arrival rate through volatile sessions.
options.D: Bound the queue at about 600 alerts — 20 per second times the 30-second deadline — reject beyond it and alert on queue depth.

items.question: How many model tiers should a new production system start with, and on what basis should that change?

options.A: One, with a second introduced only when a measured cost or latency constraint justifies the added evaluation and migration surface.
options.B: Two from the outset — a cheap tier and a capable tier — so the escalation path is already in place before it is needed.
options.C: One per pipeline stage, chosen to match each stage's measured difficulty, since that minimises cost from day one.
options.D: As many as there are distinct subtasks, so that each subtask runs on the smallest tier that can handle it.

items.question: A medical device manufacturer screens 30,000 customer complaints a month for potentially reportable adverse events. A missed reportable event costs an estimated $2,400 in regulatory remediation; an unnecessary referral costs $18 of specialist review time, and the review team can absorb up to 4,000 referrals a month. Two operating points have been measured on a held-out set. Threshold 1: 0.12% of items are false negatives, 3% are false positives. Threshold 2: 0.04% false negatives, 11% false positives. Which should be chosen?

options.A: Threshold 1, because its total error rate of 3.12% is far below threshold 2's 11.04%, and overall accuracy is the metric the regulator's inspectors will ask about.
options.B: Neither as measured: a third operating point between the two should be found and measured before committing, since both look extreme.
options.C: Threshold 2, because expected monthly cost is about $88,200 against about $102,600 for threshold 1, and its 3,300 referrals fit inside the 4,000 review capacity.
options.D: Threshold 1, because threshold 2's 3,300 referrals a month consume most of the review team's monthly capacity and leave no room for volume growth.

items.question: A truck-fleet telematics provider is reviewing a proposal to add a second retrieval-and-generation pass to its maintenance-advisory endpoint, to improve answer completeness. The proposing team presents a six-point accuracy improvement measured on a 900-case evaluation set. The endpoint's p95 budget is 1,800 ms and current measured p95 is 1,550 ms. The proposal contains no latency or cost figures. You chair the review. What should you do?

options.A: Approve it: a six-point accuracy improvement on a maintenance-advisory endpoint outweighs a latency cost the team can optimise away afterwards.
options.B: Reject it: a full additional retrieval-and-generation pass cannot possibly fit inside 250 ms of headroom, so the proposal is infeasible exactly as described.
options.C: Ask for the accuracy gain to be re-measured on a much larger evaluation set before any of the non-functional questions are considered.
options.D: Send it back for the incremental p95 and cost per request at production concurrency, so the six points can be weighed against the 250 ms of headroom.

items.question: A national postal operator is replacing a legacy rules-based parcel-exception classifier with a Claude-based one. The migration plan runs both systems over 100% of production traffic for eight weeks, with the legacy system's output continuing to drive operations while the new path's output is recorded for comparison. Which TWO capacity or cost consequences must be planned for explicitly? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: The new path must be provisioned for the full production volume from the first day of the window, even though it drives none of the operational decisions during it.
options.B: The workload's total cost is elevated for the whole eight weeks and belongs in the migration budget as a time-boxed line rather than steady-state run cost.
options.C: Provisioning for the new path can ramp gradually in line with the rollout percentage, since operational traffic transfers to it progressively over the window.
options.D: The new path's latency need not be measured during the window, because no operational decision waits on its output during the comparison.
options.E: The two paths can share a single throughput allocation without an increase, because their peaks are offset by the time each takes to process a parcel.

items.question: A news aggregator split its daily-briefing generation from one call into five concurrent section calls joined by a short assembly step, cutting p95 by about 60%. Each section call carries the same 8,000 tokens of shared source material plus roughly 400 tokens of section-specific instruction, and returns about 400 tokens; the original single call was 8,000 in and 2,000 out. Since the change, the provisioned throughput allocation now saturates at roughly 23% of the traffic it previously supported. What should the team do?

options.A: Give each section only the slice of source material it needs rather than all 8,000 tokens, which recovers most of the lost capacity.
options.B: Revert to the single call, since a 60% latency improvement does not justify a fourfold reduction in the traffic the allocation supports.
options.C: Move the five section calls to a cheaper tier, which restores the allocation headroom the fan-out consumed without touching latency.
options.D: Request an allocation increase sized to the new consumption, since the fan-out is a deliberate design choice and the extra tokens are the price of the latency gain.

items.question: A contract research organisation uses a Claude agent to draft protocol-deviation reports and file them into the trial master file system through a tool call. The applicable regulation requires a qualified person to sign off before a deviation record exists in the trial master file. The current design has the agent file the record immediately, notify a qualified person, and allow retraction within 24 hours; retraction is implemented as a superseding entry, because the trial master file is append-only. Roughly 3% of drafts are retracted. What is the correct architectural change?

options.A: Add a second Claude call that critiques each draft against the deviation-classification SOP and blocks filing when the critique disagrees with the draft.
options.B: Keep filing immediately but gate it behind a confidence classifier that holds back drafts scoring below 0.9 and routes only those to the qualified person.
options.C: Have the agent emit a proposed record and let the filing tool write to the trial master file only once the qualified person's approval is recorded.
options.D: Keep the current flow, shorten the retraction window to one hour, and add an on-call pager rota so a qualified person always responds inside it.

items.question: A motor insurer auto-adjudicates 12,000 low-value claims a day with a Claude workflow. Anything the workflow escalates goes to a queue worked by 40 adjusters whose combined throughput is about 1,500 items a day. The escalation rule is a single threshold on the model's self-reported confidence, currently set so that around 2,600 claims a day escalate. The queue has grown for three weeks and the 48-hour decision SLA is now breached on a fifth of escalated claims. A sample audit shows the escalated set is not enriched for large or contentious claims. What should the architect change?

options.A: Hire and train a further 30 adjusters so the queue clears 2,600 items a day, since the escalation rule is capturing genuinely uncertain cases.
options.B: Rank claims by expected cost of error — severity times a calibrated error probability — and escalate the top items up to reviewers' measured throughput.
options.C: Lower the confidence threshold until daily escalation volume falls to about 1,500, matching adjuster throughput and restoring the 48-hour SLA.
options.D: Add a second Claude pass with a stricter rubric that re-reviews escalated claims and releases the ones it agrees with, sending only disagreements to adjusters.

items.question: A streaming-media company renders Claude responses token by token in a support chat widget. The product requirement is a p95 time-to-first-token of 600ms. A policy classifier that must see complete sentences to be accurate was added last quarter; the implementation buffers the entire response, classifies it, and only then begins rendering, which has pushed p95 time-to-first-token to 2.4 seconds and driven a measurable drop in chat completion. The classifier itself adds about 120ms. Which design restores the latency contract without giving up the control?

options.A: Buffer to sentence boundaries, classify each completed segment, and release the ones that pass, regenerating from the first segment that trips.
options.B: Render tokens as they arrive, classify the completed response, and remove or replace the message in the widget when the classification fails.
options.C: Move the policy check to the input side only, screening the user's message before generation, since a compliant request cannot yield a violating answer.
options.D: Move generation to a lower-latency model tier and increase the streaming chunk size so the full response completes sooner and the buffer clears faster.

items.question: In a circuit breaker protecting calls to a model endpoint, what does the half-open state do?

options.A: Holds incoming requests in a buffer until the cool-down timer expires, then releases the accumulated batch to the dependency at once.
options.B: Splits traffic fifty-fifty between the primary endpoint and the fallback path until their observed error rates converge.
options.C: Admits a limited number of trial requests to test whether the dependency has recovered, closing on success and re-opening on failure.
options.D: Continues to reject all caller traffic while a background health-check ping to the endpoint decides when the breaker closes.

items.question: An online grocer shows Claude-generated substitution suggestions when an item in a basket is out of stock. Product has set a 400ms budget for the suggestion; the checkout page renders without it if it is not ready. On Saturday mornings the model call's p99 rises sharply and checkout page load has started to correlate with it, because the current implementation waits for the call with a 3-second client timeout and retries once. Which change fits the reliability profile of this feature?

options.A: Raise the client timeout to 5 seconds during the Saturday peak window so that fewer suggestions are lost while p99 is elevated.
options.B: Keep the 3-second timeout but make the retry immediate rather than backed off, so a failed first attempt still has time to land.
options.C: On timeout, fall back to a second Claude call on a lower tier with no deadline attached, so a suggestion always appears once the retry returns.
options.D: Enforce a 400ms caller deadline with no retry, fall back to a precomputed substitution table, and shed the model call while a breaker is open.

items.question: A freight broker runs a Claude agent inside a queue consumer with at-least-once delivery. One of the agent's tools posts a capacity booking to a partner carrier's REST API, which supports an idempotency header. About once a week a worker is evicted between the successful partner call and the write of the agent's own state, the message is redelivered, and a duplicate booking is created that costs a cancellation fee. The team currently generates a fresh UUID for the idempotency header on each tool invocation. What is the correct fix?

options.A: Derive the idempotency key from the booking's business identity — shipment id, leg and the invariant fields — so a redelivery reuses the same key.
options.B: Wrap the partner REST call and the agent's state write in a single database transaction so that neither can commit without the other.
options.C: Switch the queue to its exactly-once delivery mode so that a message is never redelivered after a worker eviction and no duplicate booking is created.
options.D: Have the agent query the partner's booking search endpoint for that shipment and leg first, and post only when no matching booking is found.

items.question: A litigation-support firm splits a 900-page document production into 30 parallel Claude section summaries and then runs a reduce step that composes a review memo. During provider overload, one to three of the 30 section calls typically exhaust their retries and fail. The orchestrator currently marks the entire job failed and the operator reruns it from the beginning, re-paying for the 27 to 29 sections that already succeeded. Which TWO changes give this job correct partial-failure behaviour? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Remove the retry ceiling on section calls so the orchestrator keeps retrying each failed section until all 30 return.
options.B: Persist each completed section result keyed by section id, so a resumed job re-runs only the sections that are missing.
options.C: Re-partition the production into 10 sections of about 90 pages each so there are fewer parallel calls available to fail.
options.D: Run the reduce step on whatever sections returned before the job deadline and leave the failure out of the job record so reviewers see no gaps.
options.E: Give the reduce step a per-section status input so the memo names the sections it could not cover instead of composing silently over the gap.

items.question: A benefits agency runs a Claude agent that works a single appeal case end to end: it retrieves the case file, calls four internal systems (two of which write a note back to the case), and drafts a determination for a caseworker. Runs take 6 to 20 minutes. The platform deploys daily and evicts in-flight workers, and evicted runs restart from scratch, which duplicates the notes written by the two writing systems. Which design addresses this?

options.A: Serialise the full message history to object storage every few hundred tokens and resume an evicted run by replaying that history into a fresh model call.
options.B: Checkpoint each completed step by persisting its durable output and case decision state, and make steps idempotent so a resume replays those results.
options.C: Drain workers before each daily deploy and cap any run at five minutes, failing runs that exceed it so nothing is ever evicted mid-flight.
options.D: Collapse the work into a single long call holding the whole case file in context, removing the multi-step structure that makes resumption hard.

items.question: A telco's voice self-service system must return an answer within 3 seconds at p95 or the caller hears silence. The chain is intent classification on Haiku, a retrieval call, answer generation on Sonnet, and a policy check. Each of the four steps is independently configured with a 3-second client timeout and two backed-off retries. Operations report occasional 14-second responses and rising abandoned calls, while each step's own dashboard shows healthy p95. What should the architect change?

options.A: Set each of the four steps to a 750ms client timeout, since four steps at 750ms sum exactly to the 3-second budget.
options.B: Remove the two backed-off retries from all four steps, since retries are what turn a 3-second chain into a 14-second one.
options.C: Propagate one deadline from the edge into every step, and let a step attempt or retry only if the remaining budget covers it.
options.D: Move the policy check off the critical path and run it asynchronously after the answer has been spoken to the caller.

items.question: A platform team is defining the minimum telemetry a Claude-backed step must emit before it may be promoted to production. The stated purpose is that an on-call engineer can reconstruct and diagnose one specific failed request days after it happened, in a system where the same input does not reliably reproduce the same output. Which THREE requirements serve that purpose most directly? (Choose THREE.)

options.A: A correlation id created at the edge and attached to every model call, tool call, retry and downstream span within the request.
options.B: A daily rollup of p95 latency and error rate for each service endpoint, retained for thirteen months in the central metrics warehouse.
options.C: The identity of the prompt inputs — template version plus variable values or a hash of the rendered prompt — for each model call.
options.D: The end user's raw session cookie stored on the trace span so engineers can replay the session as that user during triage.
options.E: The stop reason — end_turn, max_tokens or tool_use — and the input and output token counts returned on each model response.

items.question: An HR-technology vendor serves 800 customer tenants from one Claude-backed résumé-screening service that uses a single shared prompt template, deployed to all tenants at once. Last month a template edit caused malformed JSON for the subset of tenants whose job descriptions contained a particular delimiter. Every request for those tenants failed for six hours before anyone noticed, because the service-wide error rate rose by under two percentage points. Which change most reduces the blast radius of the next regression of this kind?

options.A: Validate the model's output against a JSON schema and, on a parse failure, issue a repair call that asks the model to reformat its previous answer.
options.B: Give each of the 800 tenants its own copy of the prompt template, maintained directly in the admin console by that tenant's own customer success manager.
options.C: Raise the sensitivity of the alert on overall service error rate so that a rise of under two percentage points pages the on-call engineer.
options.D: Version the template as a deployable artefact, roll it out cohort by cohort, and auto-roll-back a cohort whose validation failures cross a threshold.

items.question: A model endpoint begins returning overload errors for a large share of requests. The clients already retry with exponential backoff and jitter. What does adding a circuit breaker achieve that the retry policy alone does not?

options.A: It guarantees each request eventually completes by parking it in a wait queue until the dependency reports capacity again.
options.B: It stops calling the dependency once a failure threshold is crossed, so callers fail fast and the dependency gets room to recover.
options.C: It lowers cost per request by routing overflow traffic to a cheaper model tier while the primary dependency is degraded.
options.D: It desynchronises retry attempts across clients so that a fleet of callers does not retry in the same instant after an outage.

items.question: At 03:10 an airline's disruption-rebooking assistant is failing for most passengers during a weather event. The model provider is returning overload errors at a high rate. The service retries five times with backoff on every request, worker queue depth has grown steadily for twenty minutes, and passenger-facing latency is now over a minute. A deterministic rules-based rebooking path exists and is fully tested, but is disabled behind a feature flag. What should the on-call engineer do next?

options.A: Flip the feature flag to enable the rules-based path and open the breaker on the model call so requests stop queueing.
options.B: Scale worker concurrency up threefold so the queue accumulated over the last twenty minutes is worked off faster.
options.C: Raise the retry ceiling from five to eight, since the errors are transient and more attempts will convert more requests.
options.D: Open a severity-one ticket with the model provider and hold the current configuration until they confirm the cause and give an ETA.

items.question: A medical-device manufacturer uses Claude to classify whether an incoming customer complaint is a reportable adverse event. Every classification goes to a trained reviewer who sees the model's proposed classification with an Approve button. Over the last quarter the approval rate is 99.4% and the median review time is four seconds. Post-market surveillance has since found several misclassified complaints that reviewers approved. Which change best restores the value of the human control?

options.A: Grey out the Approve button for the first 30 seconds of each review so reviewers cannot click through without reading the evidence.
options.B: Ask the reviewer to classify the complaint from the evidence first, reveal the model's classification afterwards, and monitor the disagreement rate.
options.C: Require two independent reviewers, each shown the model's proposed classification, to approve before the determination is recorded.
options.D: Raise the model's confidence threshold so that only lower-confidence classifications are routed to a reviewer and the rest are recorded automatically.
